question: How many U.S. Coast Guard-approved wearable personal flotation devices (PFDs) must a recreational boat in South Carolina carry, at minimum?
choice_a: Exactly two, regardless of the number of occupants
choice_b: None are required if the boat has a throwable cushion
choice_c: Only children need a PFD; adults never need one aboard
choice_d: One wearable PFD of the proper size for each person on board
explanation: Federal equipment standards, which South Carolina's boating equipment law (S.C. Code Ann. Section 50-21-610) requires to be identical to, mandate one wearable, properly sized, Coast Guard-approved PFD for every person aboard a recreational vessel.
source_note: S.C. Code Ann. Section 50-21-610 (equipment standards identical to federal regulations); federal PFD carriage requirements (33 CFR 175)

question: Under South Carolina's personal watercraft (PWC) rules, when must occupants wear a PFD?
choice_a: At all times while the PWC is underway, since Section 50-21-870 requires every occupant to wear a properly fastened, Coast Guard-approved PFD
choice_b: Only if the water is deeper than 10 feet
choice_c: PWC riders are exempt from PFD requirements entirely
choice_d: Only the operator needs a PFD; passengers do not
explanation: South Carolina law requires every person aboard a PWC to wear a Coast Guard-approved PFD at all times the PWC is being operated, not just the operator, and not on a discretionary basis.
source_note: S.C. Code Ann. Section 50-21-870 (PWC PFD requirement)

question: For vessels 16 feet or longer (except canoes and kayaks), what additional throwable device does federal/South Carolina equipment law require beyond wearable PFDs?
choice_a: A life raft rated for ocean crossings
choice_b: At least one Type IV throwable device, such as a boat cushion or ring buoy, immediately accessible
choice_c: A second full set of wearable PFDs stored in a locked compartment
choice_d: No throwable device is ever required
explanation: Vessels 16 feet and over (except canoes/kayaks) must carry at least one Type IV throwable flotation device in addition to a wearable PFD for each person aboard, so it can be tossed immediately to someone who has fallen overboard.
source_note: Federal PFD carriage requirements (33 CFR 175) applied under S.C. Code Ann. Section 50-21-610

question: What is the key functional difference between a Type II PFD and a Type III PFD?
choice_a: A Type III is only for use on personal watercraft
choice_b: A Type II is inflatable only, while a Type III is foam only
choice_c: A Type II is designed to turn many unconscious wearers face-up in the water, while a Type III offers more comfort and freedom of movement for continuous wear but is not designed to reliably turn an unconscious wearer face-up
choice_d: There is no difference; the numbers are purely cosmetic
explanation: Type II PFDs (near-shore buoyant vests) are designed to turn many unconscious wearers face-up, while Type III PFDs (flotation aids) prioritize comfort for activities like water skiing and fishing but do not reliably self-right an unconscious wearer.
source_note: USCG PFD type classifications, universal NASBLA-aligned boating safety curriculum

question: What is a Type V PFD, and what condition applies to its approval?
choice_a: A device that never needs to be worn to count as carried safety equipment
choice_c: A device that replaces the need for any other safety equipment on board
choice_d: A special-use device (such as an inflatable belt pack or work vest) that is only Coast Guard-approved for flotation when used according to the specific conditions on its label, such as being worn rather than merely stowed
explanation: Type V PFDs are special-use devices approved only for particular activities and only when used in accordance with the approval label's conditions -- many inflatable Type V models must actually be worn, not just stowed, to satisfy the legal PFD requirement.
source_note: USCG PFD type classifications (Type V special-use devices), universal NASBLA-aligned boating safety curriculum

question: What condition must a wearable PFD meet to legally count toward a South Carolina boat's required safety equipment during an on-water inspection?
choice_a: It must be Coast Guard-approved, in serviceable (not torn or waterlogged) condition, and readily accessible -- not locked away or buried under gear
choice_b: It only needs to be somewhere on the boat, even if packed away in the original shrink-wrap and inaccessible
choice_c: Condition and accessibility are irrelevant as long as the correct number of PFDs are present
choice_d: It must be brand new with tags still attached
explanation: A PFD must be Coast Guard-approved, in good serviceable condition, of appropriate size, and readily accessible to count as compliant equipment; an SCDNR officer can cite a boater for PFDs that are damaged, undersized, or stowed somewhere they cannot be quickly reached.
source_note: Federal PFD condition/accessibility standards applied under S.C. Code Ann. Section 50-21-610; SCDNR enforcement practice

question: Why is water skiing or wakeboarding behind a boat on a South Carolina lake a situation where a PFD is especially critical, even for a strong swimmer?
choice_a: A wetsuit alone always provides equivalent protection to a PFD
choice_b: A high-speed fall can cause disorientation or injury, and a PFD keeps the skier afloat and visible to the towing boat and other traffic while they recover
choice_c: PFDs are not recommended for water skiing under any circumstance
choice_d: Skiers are legally exempt from ever needing a PFD
explanation: A fall while being towed at speed can disorient even a strong swimmer or cause an injury that limits their ability to stay afloat; a properly worn PFD keeps a skier or tuber buoyant and visible to the operator and observer immediately after a fall.
source_note: Universal NASBLA-aligned boating safety curriculum (towed water sports safety)

question: What is a common, serious mistake boaters make with children's PFDs on South Carolina waters?
choice_a: Requiring children to wear a PFD at all times on an open deck
choice_b: Checking the fit of a child's PFD before each outing
choice_c: Using an adult-sized PFD on a small child, which can slip off or fail to keep the child's head above water because it is not sized to the child's weight
choice_d: Buying a PFD specifically rated for the child's weight range
explanation: A PFD sized for an adult will not fit a small child properly and can ride up or slip off entirely in the water; PFDs must be selected by the wearer's actual weight range, not just handed down from an older sibling or adult.
source_note: USCG/NASBLA child PFD fitting guidance, universal boating safety curriculum

question: What should a South Carolina boater do before relying on an inflatable PFD for a day on the water?
choice_a: Nothing -- inflatable PFDs never require inspection or maintenance
choice_b: Store it wet and folded to save time
choice_c: Assume it works because it was purchased at some point in the past
choice_d: Inspect the CO2 cartridge, inflation mechanism, and fabric for damage, and confirm the device is Coast Guard-approved and rearming kit is not expired
explanation: Inflatable PFDs rely on a CO2 cartridge and inflation mechanism that must be checked before use; a missing, corroded, or previously fired cartridge means the PFD will not inflate when needed, so regular inspection is essential.
source_note: USCG inflatable PFD maintenance guidance, universal NASBLA-aligned boating safety curriculum

question: Besides preventing drowning, what is another major safety benefit a PFD provides a boater who falls into South Carolina's coastal or lake waters?
choice_a: It provides insulation that slows the onset of hypothermia in cold water by reducing heat loss and helping the wearer maintain a survival posture
choice_b: It has no benefit beyond keeping the head above water
choice_c: It eliminates the need to ever be rescued
choice_d: It automatically summons help without any radio or signal
explanation: Beyond buoyancy, a PFD helps slow hypothermia by adding insulating material and letting a person in cold water adopt an energy-conserving survival position (such as the H.E.L.P. posture) rather than treading water, which speeds heat loss.
source_note: Universal cold-water immersion and PFD safety curriculum, NASBLA-aligned

question: Does South Carolina law require children of a certain age to wear a PFD at all times while a vessel is underway?
choice_a: Only children over age 16 must wear a PFD
choice_b: Yes -- as with most states, South Carolina law imposes an underway PFD-wear requirement for young children below a specified age, in addition to the general one-PFD-per-person carriage rule for everyone aboard
choice_c: South Carolina has never had any PFD-wear requirement tied to a child's age
choice_d: Children are entirely exempt from every PFD rule in South Carolina
explanation: Like most states, South Carolina imposes a mandatory underway PFD-wear rule for younger children, on top of the general requirement that every vessel carry one properly sized wearable PFD per person aboard -- boaters should confirm the exact current age threshold on SCDNR's official boating safety page before an outing.
source_note: SCDNR boating safety public guidance (dnr.sc.gov) on child PFD-wear requirements, general framework confirmed; exact current age threshold should be verified on SCDNR's official page
